title: Prayer Ignites Faith
theme: Prayer and faith grow together. Even when we cannot see or feel the changes within us, God is working as we continue to trust Him.
opening: How many times have we prayed for something without receiving the answer we hoped for? We may wonder whether God is listening or whether our prayers are making any difference. But perhaps something is happening within us that we cannot yet recognize.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  Thank You for hearing our prayers, even when we cannot see or understand how You are answering them.  You know each of us so intimately. You know our needs, our weaknesses, our hopes, and the ways we still need to grow.  Lord, help me remain faithful in prayer, not simply because I am waiting for something from You, but because I want to remain close to You.  Teach me to trust the work You are doing within my heart, even when I cannot see it or feel it. When I become discouraged, give me the perseverance to continue. When I become impatient, help me remember that Your wisdom is greater than my understanding.  May my prayers deepen my reverence for You and allow Your love to grow within me. Help me become a co-worker in Your truth, extending kindness, generosity, and compassion to those who are also making their way toward You.  And when Your Son returns, may He find us still turning toward You, still trusting, still praying, and still learning to love.  Amen.
body:
Today's Gospel tells the story of a widow who repeatedly approaches an unjust judge, asking him to render a just decision in her case. The judge neither fears God nor respects anyone, and for a long time he refuses to help her. Eventually, however, her persistence wears him down, and he decides to give her the justice she has been seeking.

I have always found this parable a little difficult to understand. Why would Jesus compare our loving God to a judge who is indifferent to the suffering of another person? The judge acts only because he is tired of being bothered. Surely this is not how God responds to our prayers.

But Jesus is showing us a contrast. If even an unjust judge eventually responds to a persistent widow, how much more can we trust a God who already loves us and knows our needs?

Jesus begins by telling His disciples that they should pray always without becoming weary. And then He ends with a question that I find especially meaningful: “But when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?”

Why does Jesus begin with prayer and end with faith?

I believe there is something much deeper happening in this parable than simply encouraging us to keep asking God for what we need.

I think our persistence becomes faith. As we continue to pray, we begin to understand what faith looks like, and gradually we become what we are practicing. Prayer and faith develop together, each nurturing the other.

We may not see this happening. We may not feel any different. We may continue to struggle with the same worries, disappointments, and questions. Yet every time we return to God in prayer, we are continuing a relationship that allows Him to work within us.

God knows each of us. He knows our hearts, our limitations, and how much we still need to grow. And I believe He wants us to recognize our need for that growth as well.

There is a tremendous amount of trust involved in allowing God to work within us without knowing exactly what He is doing or when we will recognize the results.

I have often thought of prayer as bringing my needs before God, asking for His help, His guidance, or His intervention. And there is nothing wrong with that. The widow had a genuine need for justice, and Jesus does not suggest that she should stop asking.

But perhaps prayer is also about what happens to us as we continue asking.

We learn to return to God even when we are discouraged. We learn to trust Him when we cannot understand His timing. We begin to recognize that our relationship with Him is greater than any particular answer we are waiting to receive.

And sometimes, without even realizing it, our prayers begin to shape the way we live.

Today's first reading, from the Third Letter of John, gives us a beautiful example of this.

John praises Gaius for his faithfulness in helping fellow Christians, even those who are strangers to him. These people have gone out for the sake of Christ's name, and John encourages others to support them so that they may become “co-workers in the truth.”

I love that expression.

We may each have different journeys, different responsibilities, and different ways of serving God, but we can help one another continue. Through generosity, hospitality, encouragement, and compassion, we become participants in something greater than ourselves.

Our faith is no longer something we simply profess. It becomes something we live.

Then Psalm 112 speaks of those who fear the Lord and delight in His commandments.

I have come to understand that fearing the Lord is not the same as being frightened of Him. It is a deep reverence, an awareness of His greatness, His holiness, and the extraordinary love He has for us.

And I believe that reverence grows as we continue praying. It becomes wider and deeper, gradually cultivating a love that reaches beyond ourselves.

This brings me back to something I have been contemplating over the past several days: how difficult it can sometimes be to give love, even when we know how deeply God loves us.

Perhaps I have been looking too closely for evidence that I am becoming more loving or more faithful. Perhaps I expect to recognize the changes within myself as they happen.

But spiritual growth does not always announce itself.

Just as we cannot see a tree growing from one day to the next, we may not recognize how God is shaping our hearts through years of prayer, trust, disappointment, gratitude, and perseverance.

What matters is that we continue turning toward Him.

And perhaps this is why Jesus asks whether He will find faith when He returns.

He knows there will be times when we grow weary, when our prayers seem unanswered, and when the world offers countless reasons to turn away. Yet He invites us to remain in relationship with Him.

Not because God needs to be persuaded to love us, but because we need to continue allowing His love to work within us.

I find comfort in knowing that faith does not always have to feel strong to be growing. Sometimes faith is simply returning to God again, trusting that He knows us better than we know ourselves.

The widow continued seeking justice because she had not surrendered her hope. Gaius continued helping others because his faith had become generosity. And the psalmist reminds us that reverence for God gives direction to our lives.

Perhaps they are all showing us the same thing.

We become what we continually turn toward.

And if we continue turning toward God, allowing Him to work within us through prayer, perhaps one day we will discover that the faith we were so worried about possessing has quietly become part of who we are.
